# Teams, Roles, Invitations, and Federation

A team is a group of parties that share keys. Everything a team owns, its
key-value store, its chat channels, its membership of other teams, is
protected by the team's shared key, the PTK, and the PTK is boxed to each
member's own key. The hard problems are not the boxing but the bookkeeping
around it: who is a member, with what authority, as of when; how a change of
membership is proven to every reader; how a member can be admitted without
an administrator being online; how the whole arrangement works when the
team and its member live on different servers that do not trust each other;
and how a server itself can change its signing key without every client
that pinned it treating the change as an attack.

Two general techniques recur throughout, so they come first: signed
append-only chains for authority, and bearer tokens stored as hashes for
delegation.

## Two general techniques

A **signature chain** is a sequence of records where each record carries the
hash of its predecessor and a signature by a key the previous records have
authorised. [Chapter 10](10-sigchains.qmd) describes chains in general and
[Chapter 13](13-client-verification.qmd) describes how a client verifies one
against the Merkle tree. For teams the chain is the *only* authority: the
server stores links, but a link a client cannot verify is a link that does
not exist.

A **bearer token** is a secret whose possession alone grants access; whoever
presents it is served, with no further proof of identity. Bearer tokens are
convenient exactly where identity is awkward: a member of a remote host, a
client that has already proven itself once and wants a cheap handle for a
session, or a person who has been invited but has no account yet. Their
weakness is theft, so a system that issues them should store as little as
possible. The standard discipline, the same as for passwords, is
*hash-then-store*: the server keeps only a one-way hash of the token and
compares hashes on presentation. A stolen database then yields nothing that
can be presented. FOKS applies this to the session and federation bearers
described in this chapter, and where it must be able to *re-issue* a token
later it keeps the token encrypted under a server key that is not in the
database.

## Team chains

Each team has a chain of `TeamGroupChange` links. A link carries:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seqno`, `previous` | position and hash of the previous link |
| `root` | the Merkle tree root the signer observed |
| `time` | signing time |
| `next_location_commitment` | commitment to the hidden Merkle location of the next link |
| `team`, `host` | the team's ID and home host |
| `signer`, `signer_owner` | which key signed and which party owns it |
| `changes` | member additions, role changes and removals |
| `shared_keys` | new PTK generations introduced by this link |
| `metadata` | index-range allocations and other annotations |

Each member change names the party, its optional *scoped host* (for a
member from another server), the `source_role` the party used to sign, and
the new `role`. Replaying the chain yields a *roster*: for every member, its
role, the generation of its own shared key that the team last recorded, its
verify key and the fingerprint of its hybrid encryption public key, and the
commitment to its removal key (below).

Roles are ordered. A `Role` is a kind plus, for members, a signed 16-bit
*visibility* level that orders members among themselves:

| Kind | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `None` | 0 | not a member; used as the destination of a removal |
| `Member` | 1 | carries a visibility level |
| `Admin` | 2 | may edit the roster and sign certificates |
| `Owner` | 3 | may do everything an admin can, plus change owners |

Every role has its own PTK, and a member holds the PTKs of every role at or
below its own. A member with role `r` therefore receives, when loading the
team, exactly one PTK parcel for every role `≤ r`, and the loader rejects a
response with more or fewer.

## Membership changes and rotation

Adding a member is a link with a change to a positive role and a box of the
current PTKs to the new member's key. Removing or demoting a member must do
more, because the departing member already holds the PTKs it was given, and
nothing can take them back. The only remedy is to advance the generation of
every PTK the member could read and box the new generations only to the
members who remain. [Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd) explains generational
keys and the seed chain that keeps old data readable; here the question is
*which* roles must rotate.

The rule is a pure function. Given the member's old role, its destination
role (`None` for removal), and whether its own key generation is being
advanced at the same time, every current PTK role `r` rotates if

- `r ≤ old role`, and
- the member is being removed, **or** its own key generation advanced
  (its old key may be compromised), **or** `r >` the destination role (it
  is losing that role).

Promotion is refused by the rotation path; it needs a separate
key-distribution transaction, because a promotion boxes *existing* keys to
the member rather than creating new ones.

New PTK seeds are boxed only to recipients whose complete roster the client
has independently verified against current user and team chains. When a
team is a member of another team, the requirement is recursive: a parent
must not box a fresh PTK to a child team whose own PTK is still exposed
through a stale member. After any mutation the client re-sweeps the whole
local membership graph child-before-parent, because every mutation advances
the Merkle tree and recipients verified at different heads must not be
mixed.

A removal also requires the member's **removal key**: a random 32-byte
secret created when the member was admitted, whose commitment is published
in the admitting link and which is boxed both to the admin PTK and to
the member's own key. A removal is accompanied by an HMAC under that key. The
inferred purpose, consistent with the Go implementation, is that a removed
member, who can no longer load the chain, can still verify that the removal
was authorised.

## Ad-hoc and named teams

FOKS has two kinds of team, distinguished by the type byte of their entity
ID. A **named team** has a human-readable name that is committed in the
chain and bound in the Merkle tree under a name key, exactly as usernames
are, so that a name maps to one team and a client can prove it. An **ad-hoc
team** has no name. Both kinds take their ID from the verify key of the
generation-1 admin PTK, with the entity type byte marking the kind. The
server keeps a single host-wide placeholder name row (`-`) so that ad-hoc
teams can be loaded through the same code path; the verifier checks that
this placeholder has no name leaves of its own.

## Invitations

An invitation lets someone join a team when no administrator is present to
act. It rests on a **team certificate**: a payload signed by the team's
admin PTK that names the team, the admin key (generation, verify key, and
hybrid public key fingerprint), a timestamp, the admin's hybrid public key,
and an optional name of at most 1,024 bytes. What the inviter actually
shares is a **team invite**: the team's host and the typed hash of the
certificate. A joiner who receives an invite fetches the certificate from
the host by hash, verifies it, and boxes a join request to the hybrid
public key inside it. Join requests are durable rows on the server, one
pending request per joiner and role; a decision records which chain link
implemented it. The server's own comments are explicit that the chain
remains the acceptance authority: a request row is never itself membership.

```
inviter                       server                       joiner
  |-- certificate (signed) -->|                              |
  |   invite = {host, H(cert)}|                              |
  |=============== invite, out of band ======================>|
  |                           |<-- lookup by H(cert) --------|
  |                           |--- certificate ------------->|
  |                           |<-- boxed join request -------|
  |<-- pending request ------ |                              |
  |--- chain link admitting joiner, with PTK boxes --------->|
```

### The rotated-certificate signature order

A certificate carries one signature if the admin PTK is at generation 1 and
two otherwise. Signatures are *stacked*, as on chain links: the second
signature covers the payload and the first signature, so the order is part
of what is authenticated ([Chapter 10](10-sigchains.qmd) describes
stacking). For a team whose admin PTK has rotated, the certificate is signed
by the *current* admin PTK first and by the team's founding key (the
generation-1 admin PTK, whose public key is the team ID itself) second. The
founding key's signature is what ties a certificate produced after a
rotation back to the identity a joiner can look up.

The fixtures captured from the Go v0.1.9 client record what the
repository's oracle notes call a *reversed* verifier order for rotated
certificates. Rather than diverge from every existing Go server and client,
the Rust verifier reproduces that order exactly: signature 0 must be by the
current key and signature 1 by the founding key, and a test confirms that
swapping the two makes a rotated certificate fail to verify. This is one of
the compatibility quirks [Chapter 23](23-compatibility.qmd) collects.

## Session capabilities: challenges and admin tokens

Proving membership by full chain verification on every request would be
expensive. FOKS instead has a member prove membership once and then use a
short-lived bearer.

The **team-view challenge** is stateless. The server builds a challenge
containing the request, the current time, a random 16-byte token, the
identifier of the server's capability key generation, and an HMAC over all
of that under the capability key. It stores nothing: the MAC makes the
challenge self-authenticating, so issuing one costs no write. To activate
the challenge the member signs it with the key the roster currently records
for it. The server verifies the MAC, checks that the challenge is within its
6-hour lifetime, re-derives the member's current verify key from the roster,
checks the signature, and only then writes a row keyed by the hash of the
token together with an *activation hash* of the whole request, so an exact
retry is idempotent while a different activation of the same challenge is
rejected as superseded. Later loads present the token; the server looks up
its hash. The agent caches an activated token for five hours, keyed on the
profile, host, acting party and team together with a digest of the
credential (its key kind, device identity, hybrid public key and mTLS
certificate chain), so a token cannot be reused over a different
credential.

**Team-admin tokens** follow the same shape for invitation-inbox operations:
the server mints a random token bound to a team, holder, and PTK role and
generation in an *inert* state, and the holder activates it with a signature
by the admin or owner PTK over a challenge naming the token. Admin tokens
live 6 hours; the reservation that precedes activation lives 10 minutes; the
idempotency record for a completed activation lives 24 hours.

## Federation

A user on host A may be a member of a team on host B. FOKS federation is
deliberately narrow. There is no host-to-host channel at all; the README
describes federation as "Beacon discovery followed by independently pinned
remote hosts, expiring bearer grants for public user/team chains, and a
durable client-coordinated remote-team admission workflow". The client is
the courier: every step is a server-side primitive that a client stitches
together, and every server verifies what it receives with the same code a
client would use.

### Finding and pinning a remote host

A host ID is the hash-derived identity of a host's signing key, not a DNS
name. To reach an unfamiliar host the client asks a **Beacon** service for a
hint: a probe endpoint for that host ID. The hint is untrusted. The client
probes the endpoint and receives the host's *hostchain* (the chain in which
the host publishes its signing, metadata, Merkle and TLS keys), its signed
service map, and its signed Merkle root, and verifies that this material
authenticates the exact host ID it asked for. Only then is the host pinned
in hard state, and from that point the pinned hostchain is the authority
for the remote host's TLS certificates and Merkle roots
([Chapter 13](13-client-verification.qmd)). Beacon answers go into the
replaceable soft-state database as routing hints; the pin goes into hard
state.

### Remote view grants

Reading a party's chain on a foreign host requires permission. A local user
or a team's administrator asks its *own* host to grant a specific remote
party `(party ID, host ID)` the right to read its chain; for a team the
request is signed by the current admin or owner PTK. The host issues a
bearer token and the client carries it to the remote party.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Token | 17 bytes: tag byte 54, then 16 random bytes |
| Stored identity | domain-separated hash of the token |
| Stored ciphertext | token under XChaCha20-Poly1305 with the active capability key |
| AEAD associated data | domain ‖ target ‖ viewer ‖ viewer host ‖ token hash ‖ key generation |
| Expiry | `i64::MAX`: valid until revoked, matching Go v0.1.9 |

Verification on the target host needs only the hash: it hashes the
presented token and checks that a current grant exists for that hash and
that party. Decryption is needed only to *re-issue*. When the host rotates
its capability key it decrypts each grant under the old generation and
re-seals it under the new one; the plaintext bearer the remote party already
holds stays valid, which matters because that bearer may already be sealed
inside a team's PTK box on the other host. The associated data binds the
ciphertext to its target, viewer, viewer host and key generation, so a
leaked row cannot be re-bound to another target even by someone who later
obtains the key. Revocation is a permanent tombstone. A conformance test
opens the SQLite file after a grant and asserts the plaintext token does not
appear in it.

The server README describes grants as 30-day renewable leases. The code
sets the expiry to the largest representable value, with a comment that Go
v0.1.9 treats remote-view permissions as valid until explicit revocation
and that this is the compatible representation of a non-expiring bearer;
the "extend" path exists to migrate rows that were written with a finite
expiry. The code wins.

### Remote team membership

For team T on host A to admit party P from host B:

1. T's administrator grants P a remote view permission on A, so P can read
   T's chain.
2. The client allocates a **team index range** on each host and records it
   in each chain's metadata. Index ranges are rational intervals that place
   teams in a nesting order; the server rejects a joining team whose range
   overlaps, and the verifier recovers ranges from verified links rather
   than from server state. They are the boundary of the current support for
   team nesting.
3. T's administrator posts a membership link adding P with `scoped_host = B`
   and stores a **PTK view box** for P, keyed to a specific PTK generation.
4. P's members later fetch the box and open T's PTK through their own seed
   chain, which keeps working after T rotates for unrelated reasons because
   the box stays bound to the historical generation.
5. On A's public listener P's members authenticate not with certificates,
   which only A's own users have, but by signing the team-view challenge
   with the key T's roster records for P.

Remote *user* membership and general nested teams across hosts are out of
scope in the current implementation; the README enumerates the missing
pieces.

## Host key rotation

Clients pin a host by its signing key, so rotating that key is the one
change a host can make that looks, from outside, exactly like an attacker
substituting a host. The protocol makes the change slow and observable on
purpose. It takes two links and two conditions.

```
hostchain:  ... N ──► N+1 ──────────────────► N+2
                     add new key              revoke old key
                     signed by new AND old    signed by new only
                          │                        ▲
                          └── ≥ 24 h, and an operator-supplied
                              seqno equal to N+1, observed from an
                              independently syncing client ───┘
```

*Stage* creates the new key generation and a durable operation row;
repeated calls return the same operation, so a crash has a stable ID to
resume. *Begin* publishes link N+1, which adds the new key and is signed by
both the new key and the old one, together with a Merkle root that cites it.
*Complete* refuses unless the operator supplies the exact sequence number of
the add-link as observed from an independently syncing client or canary,
and unless at least 24 hours have passed since publication. It then
publishes link N+2 revoking the old key, signed only by the new key, commits,
and only afterwards deletes the old private key file, so a crash between
commit and delete is finished by re-running the command. A checker enforces
that exactly one key is active and that the staged and retiring sets match
the operation phase. The observation requirement is a social interlock
encoded in software: no automatic process can complete a rotation that no
client has seen.

## The team loader

On the client, loading a team is the verification counterpart of everything
above. The loader tries the user's PUKs newest first, preferring the one the
last pinned roster named, and for each:

1. enters the per-host pinning span so that advancing the Merkle head and
   accepting a chain under it cannot interleave with another operation;
2. advances the Merkle root and loads the chain incrementally from the
   pinned sequence number, falling back to a full load if the delta reply
   omits material it needs;
3. verifies the chain against Merkle roots authenticated for the returned
   links;
4. finds the requesting party in the roster and checks that the roster's
   verify key and generation match the PUK in use, so a stale key cannot
   open the team;
5. expects exactly one PTK parcel per visible role;
6. opens each parcel, checks the sender's hybrid key fingerprint against the
   roster, and walks the seed chain: a parcel for generation G must yield
   every generation up to G, and every opened seed must derive to a public
   key present in the verified history;
7. pins the verified snapshot in hard state, subject to the rollback checks.

Between loads, a periodic pass must decide whether any member's own key has
advanced, which the team chain's sequence number cannot reveal, because a
member's rotation advances the *member's* chain. The client batches one
Merkle lookup for up to 256 members, asking for absence proofs of the links
that would exist if each member's chain had grown; anything short of a proof
is treated as "advanced" and reloaded, so a misbehaving server can at worst
cost the client work it would have done anyway.

## Why this design

Authority lives in chains that any client can verify, so a server can
withhold but not forge. Delegation lives in bearers stored as hashes and,
when they must be recoverable, encrypted with binding associated data, so a
database leak yields nothing presentable. Challenges are self-authenticating
so that issuing them is free and only success writes. Federation needs no
trust between servers because every server verifies with the client's code
and the client carries the messages. Host key rotation is slow because the
one change a pinned client cannot distinguish from an attack must be seen by
a human before it becomes final.

## Where to look

- `foks-proto`: `identity/chain.rs` (`TeamGroupChange`, `TeamMemberChange`),
  `role.rs`, `invitations.rs` (`TeamCertificate`, `TeamInvite`),
  `federation.rs`.
- `foks-verify`: `team.rs` (chain replay, roster, named and ad-hoc name
  proofs, index ranges).
- `foks-crypto`: `invitations.rs` (certificate signing and verification,
  remote join requests), `lib.rs` (removal keys, federation token hashing,
  view-token boxes, ad-hoc team IDs).
- `foks-client`: `team.rs` (`load_and_pin_team` and its helpers),
  `team/rotation/` (`required_rotation_roles`, witnessed recipients,
  reconciliation), `team/bearer.rs`, `team/invitations.rs`,
  `team/remote_invitations.rs`, `federation.rs`, `discovery/`, `host.rs`
  (`probe_and_pin_host_id`), `change_marker.rs`.
- `foks-client-app`: `runtime.rs` (the child-before-parent graph sweep),
  `federation.rs`, `auth_cache.rs`.
- `foks-server`: `services/federation.rs`, `services/team_loader.rs`,
  `services/team_admin.rs`, `services/team_invitations.rs`,
  `host/rotation.rs`, `host/bootstrap.rs`, `keys/rotation.rs`.
- `foks-server-db`: `schema/team.sql`, `schema/federation.sql`,
  `schema/team_invitations.sql`.
